# M2-B1 — an earned workboat and first mobile refuge

Prepared continuation, not a dispatched task or acceptance. Start from the committed candidate supplied by the coordinator after the complete SPACE-1 gate. Author: **Opus 5.5 / high**. One cohesive owner may change connected production modules, art, UI, sound, migration and meaningful tests; choose the implementation and suggest improvements. Do not divide this into per-file approval requests. Root owns integration and the later fresh Sol 6.1/xhigh acceptance review.

## Player outcome

Turn the Basin investigation into something the player can use: build a Creel, make a useful cargo-versus-home choice, collect a worthwhile workboat load, establish forward servicing and return with a better setup. A new hull should change how an expedition is planned and played. It must do more than add a recipe row or reuse a generic vehicle with a different name.

This batch combines the early Creel, its first loadouts and service/refuge payoff into one playable loop. Earned Hearthline, Hush/Spindle and the remaining islands follow in M2-B; Rift/Divide/District, Mantle and both functional endings follow in M2-C. Those remain required. Do not implement an abbreviated ending or claim full-world completion here.

## Required connected behavior

1. **Earned acquisition.** C03 remains workshop/scout preparation. C05 makes the Creel/service payoff executable with prerequisite stock and a real construction cradle. A Creel-first route must not require buying a Dart. Plans are discovered through observations and records, not XP or waiting. Avoid dumping every hull and refit into the initial workshop menu.
2. **A useful workboat.** Implement the Creel's deliberate handling, cockpit/visible fittings, cargo role and physical boarding/departure. It has a240m base rating; a paid350m refit opens later Basin/Rift-shoulder work without becoming a prerequisite for its own ingredients. Preserve separate personal/hull limits. Keep the Dart faster and useful for scouting; a deeper Basin observation can justify its optional350m refit without becoming a Creel prerequisite.
3. **Real loadout choices.** Cargo rack and cabin compete for the Creel's one major utility mount. Use the fleet/candidate capacities as starting values, then justify any tuning. Swapping at supported sites preserves item identities and materials; a capacity reduction refuses or offers an explicit stow path before changing anything. Do not silently eject cargo, destroy a module or let fitted state double-count capacity. Leave a coherent path for the later powered service head.
4. **An early mobile home.** The cabin provides a physically valid fixed dry refuge with useful bunk/rest, simple cooking and persistent storage. Register it deliberately through ordinary controls. Test recovery to the registered healthy, powered, clear cabin and fallback to the pod when it is disabled, unpowered/unsafe or obstructed. Emergency air is labelled and finite. Station keeping before leaving the helm is the baseline; underway walking is not required. Earlier loadout/storage investment remains useful after later carrier acquisition.
5. **Work worth returning for.** Add authentic Basin tagged-frame handling and a paid forward-service payoff. Frames retain alloy provenance and scarce stock; they are not a ninth resource or infinitely repeatable rewards. Creel hauling should reduce transfers or enable a useful combined load, while the existing buoy/smaller-craft route remains viable for future carrier construction. Do not make the buoy or Creel an arbitrary mandatory carrier recipe dependency. Restore a Canopy service stop with useful local charging/storage/repair, tied to known observations; keep the existing lab air pocket meaningful.
6. **Finite supply and progression.** Place the specified second membrane habitat in clear-water Canopy margins, with at least two understandable matching patches, visible hosts and reachable first stock. Reconcile new recipes, hull/module investments and sources in the sole runtime registry. Prove required progress plus a credible optional purchase and failed rescue without any living renewal, reserve wait or random drop. Preserve SPACE-1 renewal rules; do not turn every new source into a respawn faucet.
7. **Connected world and local recovery.** Author enough route/landing/turning space to use the workboat and forward refuge. Include distinctive approach landmarks, safe and risky choices and a practical return. Validate actual rendered terrain against physical support, stock/host visibility and full hull sweeps. Every newly loss-capable site must have starter-accessible rescue staging and a complete Bobbin tether plus tow or in-place salvage path. Recover frame investment, fitted modules and cargo locally when both Dart and Creel are disabled; do not require a second advanced hull or delete the only progressed module.

## Compatibility and lifecycle

Evolve the state/interfaces coherently and document the final contracts. Freeze and validate the previous exact saved domain before migration; initialize only genuinely new fields/sources once. Preserve old resource stock and renewal progress, IDs, investments, knowledge/provenance, poses, notes, charge, damage, cargo, losses and journals. Never turn a diagnostic fleet into an earned campaign. Every successful paused command must be immediately saveable, and refusals must be atomic. Existing save/read/import/Continue protections, previous generation and exclusive-writer behavior remain.

Measure current first-entry/menu behavior and record explicit responsiveness budgets before judging the new results. Preserve the accepted warm50ms criterion and relevant hunter-query predicate. Exercise retained memory/eviction, multiple parked/disabled/occupied hulls, same-page state replacement, quality changes, context loss and disposal as affected. Use bounded lifetimes and useful loading feedback rather than an unbounded permanently resident world. Hardware timing claims require actual renderer/device evidence; SwiftShader does not become GPU proof after a VM RAM increase.

## Presentation and play evidence

Use the existing visual language and build a recognizable Creel/cabin/service stop in the actual game. Controls should expose the next useful action with clear labels and compact costs/state. Avoid repeated subtitles, helper paragraphs and simultaneous duplicate notices. Keep necessary warnings, captions and accessible controls. The player's view, interaction ray, collider, airway and pressure datums must agree where they are meant to; do not hide geometry problems by moving only the camera.

Deliver a source-attributed production play sequence: earned Basin knowledge → gather/pay/build → board/depart → useful workboat mission → forward service/loadout or cabin registration → return/store → actual reload/Continue. Also cover the Creel-first alternative, a mobile-refuge loss/fallback and local recovery with retained investment. Existing earned saves may shorten an affected check when clearly labelled; at least one earned new acquisition chain must use real commands and ordinary controls. Seeded edge cases are diagnostics, not proof of the full loop.

Record useful delivered cargo, collection/transfer/refit counts, unnecessary repeat hauling, and pre-refill oxygen/power minima. Conservative first-access round trips target at least25% reserve; boarding or service refill must not hide a deficient diver leg. Human feel, route learning, duration and enjoyment remain unmeasured unless humans actually test them.

Run proportional meaningful automated checks and the complete composed check/build before handoff; extend runtime economy/progression verification rather than relying only on the old arithmetic proposal. Inspect actual final visuals and relevant motion. Preserve prior evidence instead of overwriting it. No review-count inflation or redundant unchanged test loops.
